notes.meaning: The Lord commands that the inner eastern gate remain shut during the six normal working days. It must only be opened on the Sabbath and on the day of the New Moon. Keeping this gate closed during the workweek marks a clear boundary between everyday labor and sacred times of worship.

The prince enters through the porch of the gateway and stands by the doorpost while the priests offer his sacrifices. He bows down in worship at the threshold and then leaves, though the gate remains open until evening. This position shows that while the prince has high honor, he is not a priest and cannot enter the inner court to offer sacrifices himself.

On Sabbaths and New Moon days, the common people also come to worship the Lord at the entrance of this open gate. They stay in the outer courtyard, looking inward toward the sanctuary to join in worship. God invites all His people to draw near on holy days, even while preserving sacred order in His house.

On the Sabbath day, the prince must present six male lambs and one ram, each without any flaws. Under the older law of Moses, only two lambs were required for the Sabbath. This vision calls for a much larger offering, showing greater generosity and devotion in worship.

With the ram, the prince is to bring an ephah of grain, which is about half a bushel of flour, mixed with a hin of olive oil. For the lambs, the amount of grain is not fixed, but left to whatever he is able and willing to give. God accepts offerings that reflect the worshipper's ability and free heart.

On the monthly New Moon festival, the prince's burnt offering consists of a young bull, six lambs, and one ram, all without defect. These numbers differ from the law of Moses, which required two bulls and seven lambs along with a goat. This shows that the vision outlines its own special guidelines for sacred gatherings.

The prince must provide a standard grain offering of one ephah for the bull and one for the ram, mixed with oil. For the lambs, he brings as much grain as his resources allow. True devotion gives according to the blessings God has placed in one's hands.

When the prince comes to worship on these holy days, he goes in by the gateway porch and leaves by the very same way. This keeps his arrival and departure orderly and distinct from the path taken by the crowds on major festival days.

At the major appointed feasts, huge crowds enter the temple courts to worship. Anyone entering through the north gate must leave through the south gate, and anyone entering by the south gate must leave by the north. Forbidding people from turning around keeps the vast crowd moving in an orderly stream and prevents confusion.

During these great festivals, the prince does not remain apart from the community, but enters and leaves in the middle of the crowd. As their civic leader, he joins directly with the people to set an example of humble devotion. Good leaders lead by worshipping alongside those they serve.

At all appointed feast days, the amounts for the grain offerings remain uniform with the rules already given. A bull and a ram each require one ephah of flour with oil, while the lambs receive as much grain as the giver can afford. This establishes a steady, reliable standard for public celebrations.

If the prince decides to present a voluntary burnt offering or peace offering on a normal weekday, the inner east gate is opened for him. He worships just as he does on the Sabbath, but as soon as he leaves, the gate must be shut immediately. This allows for spontaneous personal praise while still protecting the sacred space.

Every single morning, an unblemished yearling lamb must be sacrificed as a burnt offering, accompanied by fine flour and olive oil. Unlike the older law of Moses, which commanded both a morning and an evening sacrifice, this vision directs a daily offering only in the morning with larger portions of grain and oil. This regular routine teaches that God's people must begin each day dedicated to Him.

differ.view: These animal sacrifices will literally take place in a future earthly temple during Christ's thousand-year reign, serving as visual memorials of His cross.
This vision uses Old Testament sacrificial language to symbolize the pure spiritual worship of the church, which is fully completed and ended by Christ's final sacrifice.

notes.meaning: If the prince gives a gift of land from his royal estate to one of his sons, it becomes that son's permanent possession. The land stays in the family as an inheritance passed on to future generations. This ensures that the royal family maintains its own hereditary wealth.

If the prince gives a gift of his land to a servant rather than a son, that gift is only temporary. The servant can keep it until the Year of Jubilee, called the year of freedom, when all leased land returns to its original owner. This prevents the prince's royal family from permanently losing their ancestral land.

The prince is strictly forbidden from seizing the people's land or forcing them out of their property. He must provide for his children entirely out of his own portion so that ordinary families are never displaced. God protects the rights of the weak against greedy rulers who abuse their authority.

The heavenly guide brings Ezekiel through an entry next to the gate and into the holy rooms assigned to the priests on the north side. At the far western end of these chambers, the guide points out a separate cooking area. This reveals the practical arrangements made for the priests during their service.

The guide explains that this is the kitchen where the priests boil the guilt offerings and sin offerings, and where they bake the grain offerings. Cooking these sacrifices within their own quarters keeps the holy food from being carried out into the outer court where the public gathers. This separation safeguards the special holiness of the offerings belonging only to God and His priests.

Next, the guide leads Ezekiel out into the main outer court and walks him to its four corners. In every single corner of the great courtyard, Ezekiel sees a smaller, separate court. These spaces were planned with a clear purpose for the broader life of the temple.

Each of the four corner courts had identical dimensions, measuring forty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. They were enclosed areas set inside the corners of the temple's outer wall. Their matching size shows the order and balance built into the entire sacred compound.

Running around the inside walls of each small court was a stone ledge or row of masonry. Built beneath these ledges were cooking hearths and boiling places. These provided durable, practical cooking stations for preparing sacred meals.

The guide tells Ezekiel that these corner rooms are the kitchens where the temple servants, the Levites, boil the sacrifices brought by the people. While priests prepared their holy portions privately, these outer kitchens cooked the peace offerings that ordinary worshippers and their families ate together in fellowship with God.
